articles.headline: OFAC Amends FAQs on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Filing Reports
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) regarding the blocking and rejecting of transactions and the filing of reports. This update is part of OFAC's ongoing review process to ensure its published guidance remains current and clear for financial institutions and other regulated entities.

The amendments specifically address FAQs 10, 32, 33, 34, 35, 36, 41, 42, 49, 50, and 53. These FAQs cover critical aspects of sanctions compliance, including the procedures for handling blocked property, the criteria for rejecting transactions, and the requirements for submitting various reports to OFAC.
This revision aims to provide greater clarity and assist compliance professionals in navigating complex sanctions scenarios, ultimately enhancing the effectiveness of U.S. sanctions programs.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Iran and Russia General Licenses, Amends FAQs, and Removes Belarus and North Korea Designations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced significant actions, including new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses, amendments to existing Frequently Asked Questions, and the removal of certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea.

Specifically, OFAC issued Iran General License GG, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving 'Karnakis and Karnakis,' and Iran General License HH, permitting wind down activities, limited safety and environmental transactions, and the offloading of cargo involving certain persons or vessels blocked on October 21, 2026.

Additionally, a Russia-related General License 131K was issued, authorizing certain transactions for the negotiation of and entry into contingent contracts for the sale of Lukoil International GmbH and related maintenance activities. OFAC also amended FAQs 1224 and 1225 and updated its Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons (SDN) List.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues Designations Under Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA) and Associated General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These designations are accompanied by the issuance of associated General Licenses to guide compliance.

While specific details of the designated entities and individuals were not immediately released in the summary, PAIPA targets those involved in the theft or misappropriation of U.S. intellectual property, a critical area of national security and economic interest.

The issuance of General Licenses alongside these designations aims to mitigate unintended consequences and provide clear guidance for legitimate transactions that might otherwise be impacted by the new restrictions.

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Venezuela-related General License for Earthquake Relief
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued an amended Venezuela-related General License (GL) and a corresponding Frequently Asked Question (FAQ). This amendment, GL 60A, supersedes GL 60 and extends the authorization for transactions related to earthquake relief efforts in Venezuela.

The authorization period for these relief efforts has been extended from its original end date of October 23, 2026, to April 21, 2027. This extension aims to ensure continued humanitarian assistance to the region.
Venezuela-related FAQ 1263 has also been amended to reflect this extended authorization end date, providing updated guidance for those involved in humanitarian operations.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Iran-related Entities, Cuba Entity, and Issues New General Licenses and FAQs
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations and a Cuba designation, alongside the issuance of new and amended General Licenses and Frequently Asked Questions.

The Iran-related designations target entities and individuals allegedly enabling sanctions evasion and sustaining Iran's military and proxy forces, including Iran-based banks Jazireh International Bank Company and Chabahar International Bank Overseas Company, which reportedly operated offshore in free trade zones.

Additionally, OFAC issued Iran-related General License FF, authorizing the wind down of transactions involving International Development Bank for Investment and Finance. A new Cuba-related FAQ (FAQ 1276) and an amended Russia-related FAQ (FAQ 1225) were also released.

articles.headline: OFAC Removes Venezuelan National Assembly President Jorge Rodríguez from Sanctions List
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has removed Jorge Jesús Rodríguez Gómez, the president of Venezuela's National Assembly, from its Specially Designated Nationals (SDN) List.

This delisting signifies a modest thaw in U.S.-Venezuela relations and indicates Washington's willingness to selectively ease pressure in exchange for political concessions. Rodríguez had been sanctioned under the Trump administration due to his ministerial roles under former President Nicolás Maduro.

While this is a targeted designation removal and not a broader sectoral oil waiver, it could incrementally improve prospects for wider sanctions relief and potentially higher Venezuelan oil exports over time, particularly if ongoing negotiations on elections, prisoner exchanges, or governance benchmarks progress.

articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals and Entities for Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Activities
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations under its counter narcotics and counter terrorism programs. These actions target individuals and entities involved in illicit activities that threaten U.S. national security.

Specifically, OFAC imposed blocking sanctions against four individuals and 11 entities in Mexico for supporting Cartel del Noreste (CDN). The designated businesses are involved in horse racing, construction, trucking, and the oil and gas sector.
This action, undertaken in coordination with multiple U.S. law enforcement agencies and Mexico's Financial Intelligence Unit, represents OFAC's largest sanctions action to date targeting CDN.

articles.headline: Bank of America Settles with OFAC for $11.6 Million Over Sanctions Violations
body: The U.S. Department of the Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced an $11,662,930 settlement with Bank of America, N.A. for 475 apparent violations of various OFAC sanctions programs.

The apparent violations occurred when Bank of America processed payments involving blocked banks, failed to appropriately prioritize alerts for customers who were exact name- and date of birth-matches to blocked persons, failed to promptly update watchlists following OFAC designations, and mishandled two business accounts associated with blocked persons due to human error.

The settlement amount reflects OFAC's determination that Bank of America's apparent violations were non-egregious but largely not voluntarily self-disclosed. The violations pertained to sanctions programs targeting Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / Caracal Security Briefings

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Settlement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics, ICC Designation, and Burma-related Designation Removal
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a settlement agreement with Pegasus Worldwide Logistics. This action is part of OFAC's ongoing enforcement efforts to ensure compliance with U.S. sanctions programs.

In addition to the settlement, OFAC has issued a designation related to the International Criminal Court (ICC) and associated General Licenses. This designation reflects U.S. policy concerning the ICC.
Furthermore, OFAC has announced a Burma-related designation removal, indicating a recalibration of sanctions against certain entities or individuals previously targeted in connection with Burma.

articles.headline: OFAC Issues New Russia-related General License
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued a new Russia-related General License. This license aims to authorize specific transactions that would otherwise be prohibited under existing sanctions against Russia.

While the specific details of the authorized transactions were not immediately available in the summary, General Licenses typically provide carve-outs for certain activities, such as humanitarian aid, journalistic endeavors, or wind-down periods for business operations.
This issuance reflects OFAC's dynamic approach to sanctions, allowing for adjustments to minimize unintended impacts while maintaining pressure on the targeted regime.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: EU Imposes Largest-Ever Sanctions Package on Russia's Military-Industrial Complex
body: The Council of the European Union has adopted its largest-ever package of listings targeting Russia, adding 820 individuals and 826 entities to its sanctions list.
These measures primarily target companies and executives linked to Russia's defense industries, as well as 77 political figures connected with the September elections in occupied Ukrainian territory.
The new restrictions aim to increase pressure on Russia in response to its continued aggression against Ukraine and its brutal military campaign targeting civilian infrastructure.
articles.source: Council of the European Union / The National Law Review

articles.headline: EU Adds Individuals and Entities to DPRK Sanctions List Over Nuclear, Missile Programs, and Russia Ties
body: The Council of the European Union has adopted additional restrictive measures against three individuals and four entities under its autonomous sanctions list on the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK).

These designations are in response to their roles in supporting, promoting, or facilitating activities that contribute to the DPRK's nuclear weapons, ballistic missile, or other weapons of mass destruction programs, as well as for violating and evading United Nations sanctions.

The new listings also target activities linked to the growing military and economic cooperation between the DPRK and Russia, including the deployment of DPRK workers in Russia, commercial and industrial cooperation, and the 'arms-for-oil' trade, all in violation of UN Security Council prohibitions.

articles.headline: EU Renews Sanctions Against ISIL/Da'esh and Al-Qaeda Until October 2027
body: The Council of the European Union has renewed its autonomous restrictive measures against ISIL/Da'esh and Al-Qaeda and associated persons, groups, undertakings, and entities.

The sanctions regime has been prolonged for another year, until October 31, 2027. The autonomous list currently applies to 15 persons and 8 groups, all of whom are subject to an asset freeze and, for individuals, a travel ban to the EU.
These measures are complementary to those imposed by the UN Security Council and reaffirm the EU's commitment to counter the continued terrorist threat posed by these organizations.
articles.source: Council of the European Union / The Brussels Times

articles.headline: IAEA Calls for Swift Return of Inspectors to Iran Amid Nuclear Non-Proliferation Concerns
body: Rafael Grossi, the head of the International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA), has called for a swift return of inspectors to Iran, warning of growing fragility in the global nuclear non-proliferation regime.

This appeal comes amidst an ongoing dispute regarding the 2015 Joint Comprehensive Plan of Action (JCPOA), with China and Russia contesting the legal standing of the 'E3' (France, Germany, and the UK) to reimpose UN sanctions on Iran.

The dispute has hindered the substantive work of the Council's 1737 Sanctions Committee and its Panel of Experts, leaving the IAEA as the primary source of independent reporting on Iran's nuclear program.

articles.headline: Thousands Flee Renewed Conflict in Ethiopia to Seek Refuge in Kenya
body: Around 36,600 people have fled into northern Kenya following an uptick in fighting on the Ethiopian side of the border, according to the UN migration agency, IOM.

Forces from the Somali and Oromia regions in Southern Ethiopia have been engaged in conflict for over two decades over boundary demarcations and resources, with recent escalations sparking a new wave of displacement.

Among those who fled, nearly 11,000 have sought sanctuary within the large compound of the Oriental Mission Church (OMC), a prominent Korean-American Christian organization based in Los Angeles, which conducts missionary and humanitarian work in Kenya.

articles.headline: OCC Announces Enforcement Actions Against Major Banks for BSA/AML Deficiencies and Debanking Practices
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has released its enforcement actions for October 2026, revealing significant penalties and orders against major national banks.

American Express National Bank was issued a Cease and Desist Order and a $350 million civil money penalty for deficiencies in its Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) compliance program, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and customer due diligence and customer identification program violations.

Bank of America, National Association, also received a $750 million civil money penalty for similar BSA compliance program deficiencies, failure to timely file suspicious activity reports, and sending wires with inaccurate transmittor name information. The OCC also issued Orders of Prohibition against two institution-affiliated parties for embezzlement.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / Crowdfund Insider

articles.headline: OCC Finalizes GENIUS Act Rule for Payment Stablecoin Issuers, Modifies Yield Prohibition
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) has finalized a rule to implement the GENIUS Act, which establishes a regulatory framework for payment stablecoins.

The final rule maintains the prohibition on issuers paying interest or yield solely for holding, using, or retaining payment stablecoins. However, the OCC eliminated the proposed rebuttable presumption concerning certain payments involving affiliates and related third parties, opting instead for case-by-case supervisory review.

This decision aims to provide flexibility in a nascent market, though some critics argue it replaces clarity with ambiguity regarding the application of the yield prohibition. The rule also establishes capital, reserve, and liquidity requirements for stablecoin issuers under OCC jurisdiction.
articles.source: Office of the Comptroller of the Currency / Bank Policy Institute

articles.headline: Revisions to the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) revises the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing two addresses associated with Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. from the Entity List under the destination of China, People's Republic of (China). This determination follows the removal from the Entity List of Arrow China Electronics Trading Co., Ltd., and the removal of six aliases for Arrow Electronics (Hong Kong) Co., Ltd. in November 2025.

articles.headline: Removal From the Entity List
body: In this rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) by removing one entity from the Entity List under the destination of Turkey.

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.
